clue.text: Union leader who met a theatrical end?

definitions.text: Union leader who met a theatrical end?

blocks.note: not a trade-union boss; the Union was the northern side in the American Civil War
not a dramatic finish; he was shot in a theatre

explanation.walkthrough: The Union is the northern side in the American Civil War, not a trade union; its president was shot at Ford's Theatre, so his end was theatrical in the most literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Lincoln led the Union as US president and was assassinated while watching a play.

clue.text: Crude fellow swaps hats with barbarian from Eastern Europe

indicators.note: a word's hat is its first letter, so swapping hats trades the V at the top of one word for the B at the top of the other

blocks.note: the first letter, the hat, of barbarian
a vulgarian is a coarse, crude person; his V is swapped out

explanation.surface: A boorish man trades headgear with a savage from the east.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the hat is the top letter: VULGARIAN loses its V and takes the B from barbarian.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulgaria is in Eastern Europe, so Bulgarian means from there.

clue.text: Melody by Verdi regularly played on the radio

indicators.note: one piece sits by, next to, the other
taking letters at regular intervals from Verdi keeps every second one

blocks.note: an air is a tune
the second and fourth letters of vErDi

explanation.surface: A Verdi tune gets regular airplay on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about opera on the radio; the definition is its last four words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to air something is to broadcast it, the same sense as playing it on the radio.

clue.text: Breathes in horrid parasites

indicators.note: horrid suggests the parasites are in a nasty, disordered state

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone inhales nasty parasites.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes "in" look like it attaches to the parasites, but it belongs to the definition, "Breathes in".
explanation.definitionFit: To aspirate is to draw in breath, so aspirates means breathes in.

clue.text: Heard about dishonest types of instruments

indicators.note: what is heard is the spoken sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: people who tell untruths; say their name aloud and it matches the spelling of a harp-like instrument

explanation.surface: Someone has heard rumours about crooked kinds of musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: "Types of instruments" wants to read as one phrase; the break comes after "types".
explanation.definitionFit: A lyre is a small harp, a stringed instrument.

clue.text: New airborne manoeuvre that doesn't need much thought

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun: something that needs little thought

indicators.note: a manoeuvre moves things around, so the letters of airborne are moved

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A fresh aerial stunt so easy it takes no thought.
explanation.walkthrough: "Airborne manoeuvre" reads as a flying stunt, but manoeuvre is telling you to move the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-brainer is a decision or task so obvious it needs no thought.

clue.text: Stared at leaders of our government letting everyone down

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their first letters

blocks.note: first letters of Our Government Letting Everyone Down

explanation.surface: Someone glared at the heads of a government that has failed everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: "Leaders of our government" looks like politicians; it takes the first letter of every word that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to stare at, usually lecherously.

clue.text: One of a pair found in Hooters?

definitions.text: One of a pair found in Hooters?

blocks.note: the surface pushes a saucy reading; the pair is the two openings of one organ
not the restaurant chain; hooter is British slang for a nose

explanation.walkthrough: Hooters suggests the American restaurant chain, and "a pair" pushes the saucy reading; hooter is British slang for nose, and a nose has two nostrils.
explanation.definitionFit: Each nose holds a pair of nostrils.

clue.text: English detective's ship used for polar exploration

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
Inspector Rebus is Ian Rankin's Edinburgh police detective

explanation.surface: An English sleuth owns a vessel that went to the poles.
explanation.walkthrough: Rebus is the detective of Ian Rankin's Scottish crime novels, so the surface's "English detective" is a pair of pieces, not one Englishman.
explanation.definitionFit: HMS Erebus sailed to the Antarctic with Ross and was lost in the Arctic on Franklin's expedition.

clue.text: Sovereign that'll keep things in line?

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun: something that keeps things in line

blocks.note: a monarch, not the old gold coin also called a sovereign
the straight edge you draw lines with, not a strict disciplinarian

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense plays on "in line": a monarch keeps subjects obedient, and a measuring ruler keeps pencil lines straight.
explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign is a ruler, and a ruler is the straight edge you draw lines with.

clue.text: Arab's opal touched curves

indicators.note: touched means slightly mad, so the letters are deranged

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, the S of the apostrophe included

explanation.surface: An Arab's opal was handled along its curved edges.
explanation.walkthrough: "Touched" reads as handled; it is the old sense of slightly crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: A parabola is a particular kind of curve.

clue.text: A wee container?

blocks.note: not small; wee is British childish slang for urine
not a box; an organ of the body that holds liquid

explanation.walkthrough: Wee looks like the Scots word for small, so a tiny box; it is also the British childish word for urine.
explanation.definitionFit: The bladder is the organ that holds urine.

clue.text: Cuban, perhaps, doesn't open false accusation

indicators.note: a word that does not open has lost its opening letter

blocks.note: a Cuban is one example of an islander

explanation.surface: A Cuban keeps quiet in the face of a false charge.
explanation.walkthrough: "Perhaps" marks Cuban as an example of a broader word, islander, which then loses its I.
explanation.definitionFit: Slander is a false, damaging statement about someone.

clue.text: Embezzle pounds and save a few?

blocks.note: to skim is to siphon off money illicitly
p is the abbreviation for pound or pounds

explanation.surface: Someone steals money and pockets a little on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: to skimp is to be sparing, saving a little here and there.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp is to economise, spending less than needed to save a bit.

clue.text: Add a bit of spice before the competitive games start

blocks.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before
to season food is to add spice to it

explanation.surface: A tip to liven things up before the real matches begin.
explanation.walkthrough: "Before" does double duty: it is PRE in the wordplay and also part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The preseason is the period of friendlies and training before competitive fixtures begin.

clue.text: Specialist to lecture without a bit of money, say

indicators.note: without says the A is taken out of teach
say means as pronounced, not as spelt

blocks.note: to teach is to lecture
a nickel is a US five-cent coin; said aloud it gives the last five letters

explanation.surface: An expert lectures without charging a penny.
explanation.walkthrough: "A" is the letter removed from TEACH, not an article; a nickel is a five-cent coin in North America.
explanation.definitionFit: Technical language or knowledge is specialist, belonging to a particular field.

clue.text: Queen's unusual palace tour, not suitable for children!

indicators.note: an unusual arrangement of the letters
not tells you to leave out the thing that follows

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing, suitable for children; it is removed

explanation.surface: The monarch's odd tour of the palace is unfit for young eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, U is the film rating meaning suitable for all ages; take it out of PALACE TOUR before rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the last Ptolemaic ruler of Egypt is one famous queen among many.

clue.text: Old soldier who got the runs?

definitions.text: Old soldier who got the runs?

blocks.note: a Roman army officer in command of a hundred men
not a stomach upset; in cricket, a batter who scores a hundred runs makes a century

explanation.walkthrough: "Got the runs" suggests an upset stomach; in cricket a batter who scores a hundred runs makes a century, and the word for a Roman officer of a hundred men fits that batter too.
explanation.definitionFit: A centurion commanded a hundred men in the Roman army.

clue.text: US state is first in table with 8 points

indicators.note: the first letter in table

blocks.note: first letter of table
eight compass points: E, N, N, E, S, S, E, E

explanation.surface: A US state tops the league table with eight points.
explanation.walkthrough: The 8 points are not a score but compass points, eight single letters from N, E, S and W.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is one of the fifty, in the American South.

clue.text: Confused insect flies up to light

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up reads the word from bottom to top

blocks.note: a gnat is a small insect
an LED is a light-emitting diode, a kind of light

explanation.surface: A bewildered bug flutters up towards a lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: "Flies" reads as the insect's movement; with "up" it tells you to turn GNAT upside down in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from knotted string to muddled thinking: both words mean mixed up.

clue.text: Irritation with back to front cooker

indicators.note: the back letter is moved to the front

blocks.note: anger is irritation

explanation.surface: Annoyance at a stove that is fitted the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: "Back to front" usually means reversal, which would give REGNA; here only the last letter moves, R going to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A range is a large kitchen stove, a cooker.

clue.text: A good look at the Tour de France, say?

indicators.note: say means as pronounced, not as spelt

blocks.note: tour is French for tower, and the tower of France is the Eiffel

explanation.surface: A proper view of the famous cycle race.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tour de France wants to be the bike race; read tour as French for tower and it is the Eiffel Tower.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: the word means as much as the eye can take in, a long, full look at something striking.

clue.text: Back in Luxembourg, get sent money for a rainy day

indicators.note: read back, from right to left
the answer is inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters luxembourG GET SENt

explanation.surface: Back home in Luxembourg, someone is sent savings.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts with the last G of Luxembourg and ends inside sent; read backwards it spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest egg is money put aside for the future.

clue.text: Uproar as nonsense raised in initially serious meeting

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised reads the word from bottom to top
in places one piece inside the other
initially takes the first letters

blocks.note: first letters of serious meeting
rot is nonsense

explanation.surface: A grave meeting erupts as someone talks rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: "Initially" applies to both following words, giving S and M to go around TOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: the weather word is used for an outburst of noisy protest or anger.

clue.text: Permit head of geography to deliver a tirade

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of geography
to rant is to deliver a tirade

explanation.surface: The head of geography is allowed to sound off.
explanation.walkthrough: "Head of geography" reads as a school department head, but it only gives the letter G.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to give someone leave to do something.

clue.text: Possibly drawing Rotherham initially in tricky cup tie

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter
a tricky arrangement of the letters
in places the R inside the rearranged letters

blocks.note: first letter of Rotherham
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Rotherham may be drawn in a difficult cup match.
explanation.walkthrough: "Drawing" plays on the cup draw that pairs football teams; Rotherham United is an English football club.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a drawing is one kind of image, and "possibly" admits there are others, like paintings and photos.

clue.text: Skin and head of Icelandic animal

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: an animal's outer covering of fur
first letter of Icelandic

explanation.surface: The hide and head of a creature from Iceland.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an Icelandic beast; the coati actually lives in the Americas.
explanation.definitionFit: The coati is a raccoon-like mammal of Central and South America.

clue.text: Make yourself presentable, and be quick!

blocks.note: to appear well dressed and tidy
a British command to hurry up, where smart means brisk

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are commands; "look smart" is a British idiom for hurry up, as well as meaning dress well.
explanation.definitionFit: To look smart is to appear well dressed, and "Look smart!" is an order to get a move on.

clue.text: Expire in golden surroundings, farewell!

indicators.note: the gold is placed around the other piece

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
to expire is to die

explanation.surface: A last goodbye from someone dying amid splendour.
explanation.walkthrough: "Golden" stands for the element gold, whose symbol is AU, split to hold DIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is French for goodbye, used in English as a farewell.

clue.text: Shows way to divide irrational denominators

indicators.note: irrational letters are not in their sensible order
ST goes into the rearranged letters, splitting them

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A lesson on how to divide by awkward fractions.
explanation.walkthrough: The maths vocabulary, divide, irrational, denominators, is all surface; "Shows" is a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Demonstrations are shows, displays of how something works.
